title: Vendor strategy: Faster building cannot eliminate integration
desc: Shows generative AI changes development economics and build-versus-buy choices while workflow fit, migration and adoption remain slower constraints.

kps.k: Generative AI is reshaping legal-tech vendors’ development economics and strategy, not just adding product features.
kps.d: The cluster centres on how vendors change internal operations, investment priorities and customer offerings in response to AI. Litera’s Avaneesh Marwaha reports higher output without headcount growth and says some development work fell from roughly two quarters to two weeks. He frames daily AI use and support automation as augmentation and reduced hiring needs, not terminations. These accounts concern software production rather than lawyer productivity. They remain management observations, and his repeated interviews do not independently corroborate the gains. Relativity’s Phil Saunders describes a different resource response: increased R&D spending, larger teams and scientist recruitment.

qs.q: We were able to take things that were maybe two quarters in length to build down to maybe two weeks.
qs.a: The Business of Law: From IP Lawyer to Investor to CEO to Legal Tech Ecosystem Builder (Avaneesh Marwaha, Litera CEO) · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: Not from a termination, but I don't think we could hire much more to keep accomplishing our target.
qs.a: Ep 293: Litera's Avaneesh Marwaha: The CEO Who Left Before AI and Returned to Lead Through It · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: Faster internal development changes build-versus-buy calculations without eliminating acquisitions or partnerships.
kps.d: Marwaha expects Litera’s historically roughly equal build-buy balance to move toward 80–90% building, favouring acquisitions that contribute data, platforms or substantial innovation rather than reproducible features. This is an intended allocation, not a completed transition. His Postalize investment illustrates the exception: an external capability could still accelerate work that would take a year internally. Reveal instead envisages transformational acquisitions alongside renewed partnerships with smaller technology companies. These strategies differ in emphasis rather than establishing a universal retreat from consolidation; Reveal explicitly says only some partnerships will become acquisitions.

qs.q: I think going forward, it's more of a 80-20 build versus buy, if you're on 90-10.
qs.a: The Business of Law: From IP Lawyer to Investor to CEO to Legal Tech Ecosystem Builder (Avaneesh Marwaha, Litera CEO) · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: So for me, data and platform is where you will see us invest net new dollars, probably.
qs.a: Ep 293: Litera's Avaneesh Marwaha: The CEO Who Left Before AI and Returned to Lead Through It · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: Vendors locate differentiation in specialised applications and workflow fit while acknowledging that model advances threaten product durability.
kps.d: Ironclad’s Jason Boehmig separates proprietary legal applications from foundational capabilities, where he favours keeping pace with frontier models. Legora’s Max Junestrand similarly describes building applications that improve as external models advance, initially concentrating on a few workflows such as Word drafting and large-document extraction. Marwaha emphasises customer co-development and fitting lawyers’ existing workflows. The counterpressure is that cheaper development also enables competitors, while better models can invalidate products: Marwaha recounts failures among startups founded in 2023. These are strategic arguments and anecdotes, not comparative evidence of durable competitive advantage.

qs.q: The models were so new and I think there was a lot of debate in the industry what the best course of action was and because we didn't have the funding and because we were the second mover, I think we just made a bet which was let's use every frontier model and let's build all of our functionality like boats so that when the tide rises, you know, everything improves.
qs.a: Max Junestrand (Legora): Raising the bar in legal AI · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: I think if you can respect the lawyers and partners workflows and what they want to be doing, how they want to work and live in that world, you've got really good longevity.
qs.a: The Business of Law: From IP Lawyer to Investor to CEO to Legal Tech Ecosystem Builder (Avaneesh Marwaha, Litera CEO) · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: Faster releases do not remove the slower work of integration, migration and adoption.
kps.d: Junestrand advocates iteration faster than quarterly but says enterprise customers still need three-month visibility because implementation follows human schedules. At 8am, Leslie Witt distinguishes completed shared-platform work for LawPay, MyCase and SmartSpend from unfinished LawPay customer migration. Reveal stresses operational and cultural integration alongside technical integration; Marwaha acknowledges that some earlier acquisitions required years of remediation. The practical implication is to distinguish code delivery from customer deployment and realised use, and to include integration and change-management work in product plans.

qs.q: But, we also work in an enterprise setting where the clients that we work with expect us to spell out where the product is going to be three months from now so that they can plan as well.
qs.a: Max Junestrand (Legora): Raising the bar in legal AI · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: I can put it in that kind of past tense, but the migration of all of our LawPay customers is a main thrust and focus of the next several months.
qs.a: Leading Product Transformation Amid Company Transformation: 8am's New Chief Product Officer Leslie Witt · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: Customer readiness supports both continuity with earlier ambitions and expansion into adjacent markets.
kps.d: Marwaha and SpotDraft’s Shashank Bijapur describe AI as enabling previously unrealised goals rather than creating an entirely new direction. Bijapur says fast-growing companies supplied more receptive early customers, based on company experience rather than an industry survey. LegalOn offers standard and customer-specific playbooks to accommodate different levels of preparation, while Everlaw stresses novice users, power users and collaboration. Luminance reports doubled corporate-customer acquisition over the preceding year, without underlying counts; this is neither revenue growth nor a doubling of its installed base. Its proposed shift toward contract analysis comes chiefly from the interviewer’s framing and receives only broad affirmation.

qs.q: Yeah, mean, so for us, this is a natural evolution of where we wanted to be but failed.
qs.a: Ep 298: SpotDraft's Shashank Bijapur: From Late-Night Due Diligence to Legal Tech Innovation · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: So there's different ways that folks can do this, but we're just trying to meet them wherever they are at in this sort of development spectrum of a playbook maturity.
qs.a: Ep 301: From Law Student Startup Founder to Global CEO: Daniel Lewis's Legal Tech Journey · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: CLM exposes a substantive disagreement over whether AI renews existing software categories or undermines them.
kps.d: Boehmig presents contract lifecycle management as a natural home for AI drafting, review and extraction, attributing growth and improving unit economics partly to these additions. He nevertheless advocates new products despite possible cannibalisation. In the Axiom discussion, SPEAKER_1 instead characterises CLM as troubled and vulnerable because of unspecified pre-existing problems, while remaining uncertain that an AI-first rebuild would succeed. That speaker discloses a stockholding and does not establish Axiom’s corporate position. Neither account supplies quantified comparative outcomes. Daniel Lewis’s observation that category boundaries are dissolving provides market context, not proof that any category will disappear.

qs.q: I certainly could imagine that the CLM is disruptible because I think it had problems even before AI came along.
qs.a: E30 - Is AI Disrupting ALSPs? Axiom CSO Catherine Kemnitz · AI-native providers · 2025

qs.q: And one of the other things that has been quite interesting is the sort of dissolving of traditional category lines.
qs.a: Ep 301: From Law Student Startup Founder to Global CEO: Daniel Lewis's Legal Tech Journey · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: Ambitious workflow redesign coexists with staged experimentation, technical scrutiny and data governance.
kps.d: Saunders contrasts agentic workflow augmentation with a standalone chatbot and places data protection and purposeful data use at the foundation. Junestrand presents the Cleary–Legora partnership as a bet on transformative workflows rather than nominal adoption. From the buyer side, Ilona prioritises AI expertise and strong data science when selecting partners. AAA’s Bridget McCormack describes a staged progression from broad access under usage rules, through useful point solutions and platform integration, to an announced AI arbitrator. These accounts suggest complementary implementation approaches, not demonstrated superiority of one approach. The excerpts do not establish the agentic workflows’ supervision requirements or the arbitrator’s safeguards and performance.

qs.q: Like we have done in the past from Andrews Asia on forward, are we really clear about the protection and principles of how we leverage data and the purpose behind our motion?
qs.a: Ep 284: Relativity CEO Phil Saunders on the Future of Legal Data, Gen AI, and the Shifting Landscape of Law · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: Not the marketing, not all these other elements, but really understanding and investing in having solid, strong, forward-looking, clean data science.
qs.a: How BigLaw Can and Should Partner with Early-Stage Startups · Law firms · 2025

vlens.an: This curated AI-native legal-provider source accepts the proposition’s core distinction between rapid AI capability and slower organisational adoption, then materially extends it with a category-level argument about CLM. Its people-first account portrays adoption as staged: the organisation waited until it understood how the technology connected to its workforce and operating approach before accelerating. The source also argues that faster AI-enabled rebuilding does not guarantee a durable product category: CLM may be vulnerable because of pre-existing weaknesses, yet an AI-first replacement is not assumed to succeed. The main internal variation is between confidence in pursuing AI once organisational fit becomes clearer and scepticism about whether AI can successfully reconstruct a troubled software vertical. These are strategic experiences and opinions, not measured evidence of adoption outcomes, CLM disruption or successful AI-first rebuilding; nor should this single curated source be treated as representative of AI-native legal providers generally.

qs.q: But, again, because we were back to being people first, the way we had to engage needed to see where the tech was landing a little bit.
qs.a: E30 - Is AI Disrupting ALSPs? Axiom CSO Catherine Kemnitz · AI-native providers · 2025

qs.q: I'm not 100% sure that as products, that the CLM is able to be rebuilt quote unquote, AI first, which I think is a separate topic.
qs.a: E30 - Is AI Disrupting ALSPs? Axiom CSO Catherine Kemnitz · AI-native providers · 2025

vlens.an: This law-firm-oriented source supports the proposition’s adoption side: GenAI is changing the calculus for early technology partnerships, while technical quality, cost-benefit assessment and internal buy-in remain important constraints on realised use. It particularly reinforces the synthesis’s emphasis on technical scrutiny and organisational adoption by prioritising robust data science over marketing and by explicitly raising how firms secure internal support for startup partnerships. Material variation lies in the type and strength of the claims: Ilona offers experience-based partner-selection criteria; the Fisher Phillips speaker places GenAI within a longer evolution of knowledge management and legal technology; and the interviewer predicts renewed enterprise-search value and argues that earlier adoption decisions may need reconsideration. These accounts do not directly evidence faster vendor development, migration burdens or technical integration outcomes, so their support is narrower than the full proposition and should not be treated as representative of traditional law firms generally.

qs.q: Not the marketing, not all these other elements, but really understanding and investing in having solid, strong, forward-looking, clean data science.
qs.a: How BigLaw Can and Should Partner with Early-Stage Startups · Law firms · 2025

qs.q: How were you thinking then, you know, as a law firm, about early adoption and early partnerships with startup companies, how did you go about making those decisions and then also getting folks on board internally?
qs.a: How BigLaw Can and Should Partner with Early-Stage Startups · Law firms · 2025

vlens.an:
The curated legal-tech vendor sources collectively support the proposition that generative AI changes software-development economics and vendor strategy without eliminating the slower constraints of workflow fit, integration, migration and adoption. The strongest direct evidence comes from Litera’s management account of sharply compressed development timelines and a shift toward internal building, qualified by selective investments or acquisitions when external capabilities still accelerate the roadmap. Legora distinguishes rapid product iteration from enterprise implementation paced by people; 8am separates completed platform engineering from unfinished customer migration; and Reveal treats operational and cultural integration as additional to technical integration.

Common reasoning is that faster coding changes what vendors can economically build, but realised customer value still depends on fitting established workflows, moving customers and data, and managing organisational change. Vendors therefore continue to use acquisitions, investments and partnerships selectively rather than adopting a universal build-only strategy. They also tend to locate differentiation in specialised legal applications and customer use cases rather than foundational models alone.

Material variation concerns emphasis, not overall rejection. Litera foregrounds productivity and build-versus-buy economics; Legora, 8am and Reveal most directly substantiate the implementation constraint; Ironclad and Everlaw stress application-level value and workflow fit; and Relativity extends the discussion toward R&D investment, data governance and agentic workflow augmentation. Some sources—such as LegalOn, Luminance and the Legora sales discussion—address only adjacent issues such as customer readiness, category change or demand, leaving their individual positions unclear. The sources provide management observations, strategic intentions and product examples rather than independent comparative validation, and this curated set should not be treated as representative of all legal-tech vendors.

qs.a: The Business of Law: From IP Lawyer to Investor to CEO to Legal Tech Ecosystem Builder (Avaneesh Marwaha, Litera CEO) · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: Because even if we can build things really quickly, the adoption and the implementation of that technology also needs to happen.
qs.a: Max Junestrand (Legora): Raising the bar in legal AI · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an: The supplied regulator, court and professional-body voice supports the proposition’s implementation core, though it does not address vendor development economics or build-versus-buy strategy directly. AAA describes AI deployment as a staged process: governed access and experimentation led to useful point solutions, organisational learning, enterprise-content integration and user-facing platform integration before the announced AI arbitrator. This sequence reinforces the distinction between building an AI capability and embedding it into operational systems and services. The main internal variation is between incremental implementation and a much more ambitious end use: point solutions and platform integration are presented as preparation for an AI arbitrator. However, the excerpt reports the implementation path rather than evidence about deployment speed, adoption, safeguards or performance, so its support is practical but limited in scope. As this facet contains one selected AAA account, it should not be treated as representative of regulators, courts or professional bodies generally.

qs.q: We then started building point solutions and we built those both because they are useful to people who use our services and useful to us as we deliver our services, but also because that helped us learn as we prepared for bigger bets.

elens.an: This source supports the proposition’s core claim that generative AI is changing vendor strategy rather than merely adding isolated features. Boehmig describes Ironclad embedding AI wherever it can create product-specific value within CLM, attributes qualitative business benefits to that integration, and argues that the company must risk self-disruption and possible cannibalisation. He also supports the cluster’s account of differentiation shifting toward specialised legal applications while vendors keep pace with external foundational models. The material adds a CLM-specific perspective: AI may strengthen an established software category even as it creates pressure to launch potentially disruptive products. However, it does not address faster software development, build-versus-buy choices, or the proposition’s important qualification that migration, workflow integration and customer adoption remain slower constraints. Its business-benefit claims are management assessments without quantified or independent causal evidence.

The curated 2025 sources collectively support the proposition that generative AI is changing legal-tech development economics and vendor strategy while leaving integration, migration and adoption as slower constraints. Litera’s Avaneesh Marwaha reports sharply compressed software-development timelines, greater output without headcount growth and a planned shift toward internal building; he nevertheless retains selective investments or acquisitions where external capabilities materially accelerate the roadmap. Reveal likewise expects acquisitions and smaller-company partnerships to coexist, showing that faster building does not produce a uniform retreat from external growth strategies.

The clearest common reason for support is the distinction between producing technology and putting it into effective use. 8am describes its shared product platform as completed while customer migration remains unfinished. Reveal distinguishes technical and product integration from operational and cultural integration, and Litera reports that remediation of some acquired technology took years. SpotDraft, LegalOn, AAA and the buyer-side partnership discussion add adoption-related variation: customer receptiveness differs, products may need to accommodate different levels of readiness, and implementation may proceed through governed experimentation, point solutions and technical scrutiny.

There is material variation in strategic emphasis. Litera advocates a pronounced build-first shift; Reveal continues to favour consolidation and partnerships; Relativity responds by expanding R&D capacity and grounding agentic workflows in data principles; Legora stresses transformative workflow redesign; and the Axiom discussion questions whether CLM can successfully be rebuilt AI-first. Some sources address only adjacent matters—such as sales interest, customer growth or blurred product categories—so their position on the full proposition remains unclear. Much of the evidence consists of management accounts, intentions and qualitative experience rather than independent performance measurements. Repeated Marwaha interviews reflect the same company perspective and do not independently corroborate Litera’s claimed gains. Because the corpus is curated, these positions should not be treated as representative of all vendors, buyers or legal-service organisations.

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources support the proposition that generative AI is materially changing vendor strategy while practical adoption and workflow fit remain constraints. Junestrand provides the strongest direct support: Legora designs its application layer around improving frontier models and accelerates iteration, yet still plans around enterprise customers’ slower implementation cycles. Shankar similarly treats generative AI as a strategic step change but grounds development in users’ concrete problems rather than long-range technological speculation. There is material variation in emphasis: Junestrand addresses development cadence, application-layer differentiation and the gap between building and adoption, whereas Shankar focuses on user-led product design and offers no evidence about integration, migration or build-versus-buy decisions. Both accounts are vendor executives’ strategic descriptions rather than comparative performance evidence, so they support the proposition without establishing how broadly these patterns apply.
